basis: Existing owner-authored portfolio scope, repository artifacts and individually reviewed Figma exports. Design intent is not a measured outcome.

projects.title: Orkest HQ
projects.category: Enterprise SaaS · CRM and shared workspace patterns
projects.summary: A shared interface language for business software, with CRM screens that make ownership, qualification and the next action easier to inspect.
context: Orkest brings CRM, sales, inventory and finance into a modular workspace. My challenge was to give that breadth a coherent structure without making every module behave like the same administrative table. A lead, an invoice and a stock movement can share navigation conventions while asking very different questions of the person using them.

My contribution covered the workspace architecture, navigation levels, record and table patterns, action hierarchy and information density. This case uses the current-labeled CRM frames in the supplied primary design file as its visual evidence. Other modules and draft states are part of the broader design context; they are not presented here as completed production features.
constraints: Shared navigation must help people move between modules without erasing the task context.
Dense record lists need enough structure for comparison, while creation and review need a clearer action hierarchy.
A visible filter, view or button does not establish its implemented behavior or authorization rules.

decisions.heading: Separate ownership from record qualification
body: The leads design places All leads, My leads and Unassigned near search and Filters. These views describe ownership; qualification is represented inside the record list. Keeping those concepts separate gives a reviewer two useful questions: whose work is this, and what state is it in?

That separation also sets a handoff requirement. Switching an ownership view should have an explicit rule for existing filters, selection and the result count. The screenshot establishes the hierarchy, while the behavior still needs an agreed contract.

The complete filter sequence adds the next part of that list story: choose criteria, review a problem and inspect the resulting confirmation. These supporting form states are shown as designed scenarios alongside the current-labeled CRM core, not as proof of server behavior.
decisions.leadIn: First, the list has to explain whose work is visible.
decisions.tradeoff: Quick ownership views reduce navigation effort, but need clear rules for filters and selection when the view changes.

decisions.heading: Make dependencies visible before saving
body: The create-lead design groups contact information and qualification instead of scattering both across an undifferentiated form. Its side panel explains the capture-to-conversion sequence and says that the score is calculated after saving. That is a useful boundary: the interface should not imply that an unsaved value is already a reliable qualification result.

The remaining design-to-engineering questions are concrete: what may a draft omit, when is duplicate checking performed, who may assign an owner, and which values survive a failed save? Those questions belong beside this form rather than in a separate generic handoff document.
decisions.leadIn: Once a lead needs to be added, the interface changes from comparison to careful entry.
decisions.tradeoff: Grouping reduces visual competition; it also makes the required-versus-draft distinction more important.

decisions.heading: Reuse grammar where the operational job repeats
body: The shared system is a set of rules for location, records, status and action priority. It should reduce relearning when someone moves from a list into a detail view. It should also permit an exception when a module needs a different sequence or a more consequential review step.

I would judge reuse by whether the next task remains understandable, not by counting identical cards. For CRM, that means keeping the record identity and owner legible while allowing qualification and conversion to receive their own treatment.

The current lead-detail panel makes conversion readiness explicit: core information is complete, and conversion should preserve history while creating a contact and opportunity. That visible promise gives engineering a concrete consistency rule to implement and test.
decisions.leadIn: Saving is an intermediate step. The next design problem is moving the record forward without losing its context.
decisions.tradeoff: Shared components help orientation, while conversion needs its own consequential action and data rules.

projects.delivery: The useful handoff unit is a record workflow: entry conditions, data requirements, state changes and recovery, supported by reusable interface patterns. The reviewed exports show the visible design; they do not verify server validation, access control or synchronization between modules.
projects.outcome: Ownership views, qualification and conversion are the central CRM decisions in this case. The current screens make those relationships inspectable. A useful task review would follow an unassigned lead through capture and conversion, including a failed save; no task-time or adoption measurement is available.

journey.question: How can one workspace support different business jobs without making people relearn the interface at every module?
journey.opening: The CRM story starts before a form is opened: someone needs to recognize which leads require their attention. From there, capture should establish a usable record, and conversion should carry its history forward. I used that path to connect navigation, table hierarchy and action design instead of treating them as separate screens.
journey.reflection: The important consistency is continuity of work. Reusing a table is useful only if ownership, qualification and the next action keep their meaning as a record moves forward. I would extend the shared grammar module by module, with explicit exceptions where the business object changes.

evaluation: Find an unassigned lead, apply a filter and switch ownership views. Can the person explain which records are now included?
Follow a failed save into retry and conversion. Check that ownership, input and record history survive each transition.

projects.title: piHub
projects.category: Fintech · Creditor, investor and administrator journeys
projects.summary: Financial workflows organized around what has been submitted, who needs to act and what remains unresolved.
context: piHub spans creditor, investor and administrative experiences. The recurring interaction problem is uncertainty: a person may have supplied information but still be waiting on verification, review or another party. A short status label is useful only when its meaning and the next available action are clear.

My existing portfolio scope covers applications, credit requests, verification, account management and dashboards. I worked on information hierarchy, forms, state language and the relationship between a process state and the action available to each role. The role prototypes are separate artifacts; they do not constitute a synchronized financial application.
constraints: The same financial process is viewed by people with different tasks and permissions.
Application data and sample financial values must not be mistaken for verified transactions or product results.
A process can legitimately require waiting; the interface must explain that boundary rather than invent progress.

decisions.heading: Keep application state in the comparison view
body: The creditor journey starts with company information, moves into a product application and returns to a list of submitted work. Each screen answers a different question: who is applying, what is being requested and what happens next.

Keeping written status alongside service, industry, dates and amounts lets someone compare applications without opening every record. The complete screens retain their original dummy values so the hierarchy can be judged in context.
decisions.leadIn: The creditor’s first need is an overview of what has already been submitted.
decisions.tradeoff: A table supports comparison but cannot replace a specific explanation of an individual application’s requirements.

decisions.heading: Share status language without flattening the roles
body: The investor side changes the job. Account entry leads into defining an offer, comparing products and reviewing incoming credit requests. Reusing the creditor’s exact information hierarchy would hide that difference in responsibility.

The connection between roles is the state model, not an identical table. A review should follow one application across those surfaces and check that Submitted, Reviewing and Approved mean the same event while each role sees the information it needs.
decisions.leadIn: That view is only one side of the process. Investor priorities require a different object and information hierarchy.
decisions.tradeoff: Consistent status language supports cross-role understanding; identical columns would obscure the different jobs.

decisions.heading: Give review and recovery their own requirements
body: A verification request should say what information needs attention and preserve what is already valid. A waiting state should identify the dependency when that information can safely be disclosed. An error should distinguish a correctable input problem from a service interruption.
Those are acceptance conditions for the workflow, not financial promises. They make the handoff discussion more useful than a blanket requirement to make the onboarding shorter.

The administrator source also contains an access-denied design with a Go Back action. That is a proposed recovery surface. The account and server still need to decide whether a direct request is allowed; an error screen does not establish that enforcement.
decisions.leadIn: The journey also needs a boundary: some actions or records are not available to the current account.
decisions.tradeoff: Recovery copy should be useful without exposing restricted record details.

projects.delivery: I organize the discussion around role, current state, outstanding requirement and next action. The linked creditor, investor and admin prototypes provide paths for inspecting the design. Production permissions, uploads, persistence and real financial processing require separate engineering verification.
projects.outcome: The role split is visible in the artifacts: creditors submit applications, investors manage products and requests, and administrators review access and records. The remaining evaluation is whether the same status has a consistent meaning across those roles and whether a person knows who must act next.

journey.question: How does a financial workflow remain understandable when the next step belongs to another person?
journey.opening: For piHub, the journey is not a straight line from application to approval. It crosses creditor, investor and administrator roles, and includes legitimate waiting. I organized the case around that handover: make the current state visible, keep each role’s job distinct, and explain what happens when a person cannot continue.
journey.reflection: The state model is part of the product experience. A shorter form cannot compensate for a person who has submitted information and no longer understands who is responsible. The next evaluation should trace one application across the role boundaries, including a request for changes.

evaluation: Ask a creditor to identify who owns the next step after submission and what would require a response.
Trace an application returned for changes across creditor, investor and administrator views; check that their status language describes the same event.

projects.title: Yarsha
projects.category: Mobile · Web3 messaging and wallet context
projects.summary: Keeping contact, asset selection and consequential actions understandable inside a conversational product.
context: Yarsha brings a contact directory, conversation, shared groups and wallet-related actions into one mobile product. Those activities can begin with the same person but require different levels of attention. Finding a friend is lightweight; choosing an asset or inspecting a transaction needs a more deliberate check.

My product-design contribution focused on how those surfaces connect: identity before conversation, context before action, and a clear place to return. The following walkthrough uses complete frames from the supplied Final Mobile Design page. It follows the designed experience rather than claiming that these frames document a research timeline or a shipped financial service.
constraints: Wallet and network behavior extends beyond the messaging interface.
Asset labels and transaction context must remain distinguishable from decorative chat content.
Contacts, balances and identifiers in a design file may be sensitive even when they are sample content.

decisions.heading: Start with recognition, then handle the miss
decisions.leadIn: Before any conversation or transfer, the person needs confidence that they have found the right contact.
body: The directory pairs display names with shortened wallet identifiers. A name helps recognition; the identifier distinguishes people whose names or avatars may be similar. Search and the add-contact action sit inside the same contact model instead of sending the person into an unrelated wallet screen.

The empty-result state is part of that first step. The query and keyboard remain visible while Contacts and Invite offer different routes forward. That preserves the effort already made, but it also exposes a decision to resolve: when should the product suggest revising a query, adding someone or inviting them?
decisions.tradeoff: Familiar names reduce effort, while wallet precision and explicit recovery prevent familiarity from becoming ambiguity.

decisions.heading: Keep a conversation connected to its identity and history
decisions.leadIn: After recognition, the product can shift from finding someone to understanding the relationship.
body: The conversation keeps the contact identity in its header and the composer at the bottom, leaving the middle for shared history. The profile then gives that identity more depth through a wallet address, media, groups and links. These surfaces give different answers to the same question: who am I interacting with?

In-thread search adds a second way to recover context. It retains the conversation and provides a match count with previous and next controls. A person looking for an earlier link should not have to abandon the thread and reconstruct the search elsewhere.
decisions.tradeoff: A familiar chat layout supports continuity, but profile and search details must remain reachable without crowding the primary conversation.

decisions.heading: Change the pace when the action concerns an asset
decisions.leadIn: The familiar social context now gives way to a decision that needs greater precision.
body: Send Money begins with a username or wallet-address search and recognizable contacts. Asset selection then separates tokens from NFTs. That order makes the recipient and the asset distinct decisions rather than compressing everything into a single ambiguous action.

Tokens use names, symbols and balance-like sample values; NFT collections use artwork and collection names. The visual treatment follows the object being selected. Before authorization, the implementation still needs a review that reconciles recipient, network, asset and amount, including unavailable assets and similarly named items.
decisions.tradeoff: Different asset types need different selection patterns, while a shared review model must preserve the identity and consequence of the action.

decisions.heading: Make membership and sharing understandable
decisions.leadIn: A relationship can expand from one person into a shared space with its own responsibilities.
body: Group creation starts with member selection. The detail screen then exposes the group identity, description and member roles alongside shared-content tabs. The interface changes from choosing participants to understanding the space they now share.

The invitation screen isolates the link and provides Copy and Share as separate actions. That makes distribution explicit. A complete group model also needs decisions about who can invite, what an invite grants, and how a person understands that access before joining.
decisions.tradeoff: Easy sharing helps a group grow; explicit roles and invitation scope keep membership understandable.

decisions.heading: Give the consequential action an inspectable record
decisions.leadIn: The story ends with a detail view someone can return to and question.
body: The transaction-detail frame separates spent and received assets from the destination and network fee. An explorer action provides a route beyond the in-app summary. The hierarchy should help a person connect the summary to the underlying event rather than merely display a success-looking card.

The original frame contains a Blastscan label within a Solana-oriented design context. I retain that source detail rather than silently correcting the screenshot. It is a concrete handoff issue: the intended network, explorer destination and pending or rejected states need to agree before implementation.
decisions.tradeoff: A concise summary is useful only when its destination, network and evidence remain traceable.

projects.delivery: Twelve complete original frames make the designed path inspectable from contact discovery through conversation, asset selection, group membership and transaction detail. Dummy content is shown unchanged under the owner’s publication authorization. Wallet authorization, transaction execution and cross-device state remain integration work.
projects.outcome: The design account now exposes the relationships between the app’s social and financial surfaces. The strongest questions are continuity questions: whether the person, asset and group context remain clear at the handoff between screens. No adoption or transaction-performance measurement is reported.

journey.question: How can a familiar conversation become the starting point for Web3 actions without making every action feel equally casual?
journey.opening: The journey begins with a person, not a wallet balance. A contact becomes a conversation; that conversation can lead to shared content, a group or an asset-related action. I organized the case around the moments when the interface needs to preserve familiarity and the moments when it needs to ask for more attention.
journey.reflection: The system works as a relationship between surfaces: names help recognition, wallet identifiers add precision, and review states explain consequence. The most useful consistency is not identical layout everywhere. It is being able to move between these contexts without losing who or what the action concerns.

evaluation: Ask someone to detect an incorrect recipient, asset or network before authorizing a transfer.
Exercise rejection, a delayed confirmation and returning from an explorer. Check whether retrying could accidentally duplicate the action.

projects.title: Zapp Today
projects.category: Mobile logistics · Customer, driver and operations
projects.summary: Different interfaces for people booking a delivery, carrying it out and resolving exceptions around it.
context: A delivery creates shared state but different priorities. A customer needs to prepare a request and understand what happens next. A driver needs a clear operational task. An operations team needs the context required to investigate an exception. My existing project scope covers these related journeys, rather than one app screen in isolation.

This case uses the supplied Zapp 2.0 customer iOS file as its primary visual source. Historical customer and driver prototypes remain separately labeled. I have not combined those older screens with the newer design and presented the result as one approved release.
constraints: Customer and driver priorities differ even when they refer to the same delivery.
Maps, location, pricing and live tracking require real services; a prototype cannot establish their accuracy.
The current source contains QA and experimental frames, which are withheld from the public illustration set.

decisions.heading: Make account entry an understandable choice
body: The account-entry frame distinguishes Create account from Sign in and gives each a short explanation. The primary action gives the new-customer path more emphasis without hiding the returning-user route.
That is a narrow but useful decision to inspect. It shows onboarding hierarchy, not evidence that registration became faster or that the full delivery service was implemented.

The complete account sequence shows how that choice leads into registration and code verification. The important continuity is what survives the transition: the entered mobile number, a clear resend route and an explanation of what the next action will do.
decisions.leadIn: Before the delivery request, account entry needs to make the two starting paths understandable.
decisions.tradeoff: A dominant new-account route helps first-time customers, while returning users still need a visible sign-in path.

decisions.heading: Ask for parcel context at the point it matters
body: The parcel-details frame presents Documents, Small parcel and Large parcel with short descriptions, then asks for contents. Its visible step indicator places the task inside a longer request. The action says Choose delivery service, which tells the customer what the next screen is for.

This structure keeps package description separate from the choice of service. Before implementation, the team still needs rules for unsupported items, size limits, edited answers and validation. The screenshot shows the proposed sequence rather than proving those rules exist.

Home gives the request its starting context, parcel details establish what is being carried, and service selection turns that information into a timing choice. Showing these frames together makes the booking sequence visible instead of treating the parcel screen as an isolated form.
decisions.leadIn: After entry, the question becomes what the service needs to know about the item.
decisions.tradeoff: Early parcel context makes the next service choice meaningful; unnecessary fields would slow down booking.

decisions.heading: Review one lifecycle across the role boundaries
body: The driver stop-order screen distinguishes a confirmed pickup from the next drop-off. It shows progress and separates arrival from an intermediate-stop issue. The screen explicitly says navigation is inactive in the prototype, so I present it as a proposed task sequence.

This makes a cross-role review more specific: confirm which stop is current, which event changes its state, and what the customer or operations team should see after an issue. Separate screens still need synchronized data and real routing before that lifecycle can be called implemented.
decisions.leadIn: The viewpoint now changes from preparing a request to carrying out a stop.
decisions.tradeoff: A focused current-stop action supports execution, but exception reporting must remain reachable.

decisions.heading: Separate delivery completion from settlement
body: The driver completion frame names the completed handoff, offers a return to availability and states that settlement and earnings require verified server records. Those are different responsibilities, and the completion message keeps them separate.

For acceptance testing, I would check an interrupted handoff, a duplicate completion attempt and the return-to-dashboard state. The sample frame provides the wording and hierarchy to inspect; it does not establish that a delivery or payment occurred.
decisions.leadIn: The final moment is not simply a success graphic: it must explain which responsibility has ended.
decisions.tradeoff: A clear completion message closes the operational task without making unsupported payment promises.

projects.delivery: The handoff combines customer parcel entry with driver stop progress and completion states. Routing, delivery estimates, payments and updates across roles remain integration requirements. The screenshots describe the prototype sequence and its stated limits.
projects.outcome: The customer and driver views give the delivery lifecycle different priorities. Parcel entry, the next stop and the completion boundary can now be inspected in the case itself. A working routing or dispatch service, and any improvement in delivery performance, require evidence beyond these designs.
related: Review the full journey before redesigning

journey.question: How can the same delivery feel clear to the person booking it and the person carrying it out?
journey.opening: I treated the delivery as a shared lifecycle with different viewpoints. A customer first establishes an account and describes the parcel. A driver later needs the current stop and a clear completion boundary. Reading those moments together reveals the handovers that isolated mobile mockups tend to hide.
journey.reflection: The most consequential design work sits between the roles. A customer-facing milestone and a driver action must describe the same event, while delivery completion and financial settlement remain separate. The prototype makes those distinctions visible; a service review must still exercise delayed, failed and duplicate events.

evaluation: Compare the customer milestone with the driver action for pickup, arrival and completion; each pair should describe the same service event.
Walk through an intermediate-stop failure and delayed completion update. Check that the next action remains clear without implying settlement has occurred.

projects.title: Morajaa
projects.category: B2B consulting · Service and sector website
projects.role: UX, content structure and website design contribution
projects.summary: Helping a prospective client move from a recognizable business problem to a specific consulting service and a useful conversation.
context: Morajaa presents consulting services and sectors to visitors who may know their business problem before they know the consultancy's terminology. My contribution covered information architecture, service and sector page structure, responsive composition and inquiry paths.

The source for this case is the supplied Final Design v2 page. The reviewed example comes from the Market Entry in Saudi Arabia service design. It is a design artifact, not independent verification of the consultancy's legal claims, service performance or client results.
constraints: Service and sector categories need to connect without making visitors read duplicate pages.
Long-form explanation must remain scannable without reducing an involved service to a slogan.
A page should communicate the consultancy's scope without turning the portfolio into a source of regulatory advice.

decisions.heading: Make the service concrete before asking for an inquiry
body: A consulting category becomes more useful when a visitor can see the work involved. The market-entry design moves from an introduction into setup services, ongoing support and a named process. That sequence gives the call to action more context than a standalone contact button.

My editorial priority is the relationship between those sections. The first scan should establish relevance; deeper reading should explain the scope and sequence well enough to support a more informed inquiry.
The complete homepage gives this opening its wider context: the service offer, sector content and routes to deeper evaluation are part of one reading path.
decisions.leadIn: The opening needs to earn attention by making the service recognizable.
decisions.tradeoff: A concise introduction helps scanning but must lead into service depth rather than replace it.

decisions.heading: Use a process section to reveal the shape of the engagement
body: The source design breaks the process into named stages, including entry planning, sector feasibility and operationalization. The stage titles carry the scan; supporting text supplies detail. A visitor can inspect the structure before committing to reading every paragraph.

The complete service page shows how the process connects to the opening, capabilities, imagery and contact path. The consultancy's process wording is shown as source content; the portfolio does not endorse it as legal or regulatory guidance.
decisions.leadIn: Once relevance is established, the visitor needs a more concrete picture of the work.
decisions.tradeoff: A staged process makes a long engagement scannable while supporting detail preserves its complexity.

decisions.heading: Allow more than one sensible entry path
body: Services describe the kind of support offered, while sectors describe the visitor's operating context. Both can be useful routes into the same business. The design task is to connect them without forcing one taxonomy to stand in for the other.
On smaller screens, that relationship needs descriptive links and a deliberate reading order. Stacking a desktop layout is not enough if the explanation and its supporting action become separated.

The construction-sector page carries the same idea into a more specific context. Its job is to translate the broad offer into a recognizable sector need, then retain a route into the relevant service and contact.
decisions.leadIn: A visitor may arrive by service or by sector, so the page must reconnect those paths.
decisions.tradeoff: Two entry taxonomies broaden access; descriptive crosslinks prevent duplicate explanation.

projects.delivery: The deliverable is an information structure and responsive visual system that can accommodate service depth. The linked prototype remains an interactive reference; the images here are readable crops of individual source screens. I have not treated every page on the file's canvas as approved marketing material.
projects.outcome: The complete service page makes the content decision visible: named stages let a visitor scan the engagement before reading its detail. The next question is whether someone can choose the relevant service and explain its scope without a sales presentation. Inquiry performance has not been measured for this case.

journey.question: How can a visitor evaluate a complex consulting engagement before speaking to sales?
journey.opening: The useful journey begins with a business situation, not with the consultancy’s service taxonomy. I connected the page sequence around three questions: is this relevant to me, what does the engagement involve, and where can I go next? The complete homepage, service and sector pages show that progression at three levels of detail.
journey.reflection: For a service website, clarity is the progression from a broad promise to an inspectable scope. The process is useful because it gives a visitor something concrete to evaluate. Its commercial and regulatory statements still belong to the consultancy, and inquiry conversion is not measured here.

evaluation: Ask a prospective client to identify the relevant engagement stage and explain what the consultancy would deliver.
Check whether the process section answers the question raised by the service promise before the visitor reaches contact.

projects.title: Masteriyo
projects.role: Product UI and UX contribution within a team
projects.summary: Designing authoring and learning interactions inside an established LMS, while keeping the contribution boundary clear.
context: Masteriyo brings course creation and learning into an established WordPress LMS. A creator organizes sections, lessons and assessments; a learner encounters the resulting sequence. My product UI and UX contribution was part of the wider team’s work, including course and quiz flows and reusable interaction patterns.

This case follows the authoring side through four screens from the supplied primary file. They are team design artifacts that I have permission to present with attribution. They do not establish sole authorship of the product, or measured changes in learner completion.
constraints: Work within an existing WordPress LMS and the wider product team’s conventions.
Expose different levels of content without confusing course structure with question configuration.
Keep the team contribution explicit and treat save, scoring and keyboard behavior as implementation requirements.

decisions.heading: Make a blank course actionable
body: The empty builder offers Add Section, Add Assignment and Add Quiz, with documentation below. Rather than describing an absence, it gives the author concrete ways to begin. The design places help beside creation without making documentation a prerequisite.

The unresolved hierarchy is worth examining: the three actions have equal visual weight even though a section and an assessment belong to different levels of the content model. A first-use review should establish whether authors know which one to choose.

Course title and description give the object an identity before the empty builder asks the author to add content. Together, the frames show a transition from defining a course to making its first structural decision.
decisions.leadIn: An empty course is the first authoring task, not a dead end.
decisions.tradeoff: Several creation routes expose capability, but equally weighted buttons leave authors to choose the appropriate starting unit.

decisions.heading: Let the outline carry the course structure
body: The populated builder groups lesson rows inside an Introduction section. A section-level menu and collapse control are separate from each lesson’s edit, duplicate and delete actions. Add New Content stays inside the group; Add New Section sits outside it. That spatial distinction communicates the parent-child relationship.

Reordering is visible through drag handles, but the design still needs a keyboard alternative and meaningful names for compact actions. The header also shows Course selected while the screen contains builder content; that active-state inconsistency belongs in the implementation review.

Section and lesson editors then reveal the next levels of detail. The outline remains the organizing model while the fields change to suit the selected object. That relationship is more useful than forcing every editor into an identical form.
decisions.leadIn: Once content exists, the interface must explain how it belongs together.
decisions.tradeoff: Compact row actions preserve a readable outline; their icons need names, focus states and safe destructive behavior in implementation.

decisions.heading: Introduce quiz complexity in stages
body: Quiz setup separates Info, Questions and Settings. The first surface asks for a name and description and provides Next and Cancel. It establishes the assessment before introducing the denser work of writing and configuring questions.

The sequence needs an explicit state contract: what Next validates, whether a partially written quiz can be saved, and what Cancel discards. These are requirements for completing the interaction, rather than behaviors proved by a static frame.
decisions.leadIn: A quiz adds a different configuration task inside that course structure.
decisions.tradeoff: Tabs break the setup into parts, while each step still needs clear completion and validation rules.

decisions.heading: Keep question detail connected to its place in the quiz
body: The question editor keeps the list of questions above the expanded question. Within that editor, question type and points are separate from answer rows. Required and Randomize settings sit below the answers. This gives the author several layers of context without opening an unrelated screen for every adjustment.

For a true-or-false question, the selected correct answer must remain understandable beyond its green treatment. Reorder controls, duplication, deletion and saving need the same interaction conventions as the broader authoring system. That consistency is where a team contribution becomes easier for others to continue.

The multiple-choice example makes the reuse question concrete: question identity and points remain familiar, while the answer configuration changes with question type. The complete frames expose both the shared pattern and the extra density that each type introduces.
decisions.leadIn: Question editing is the deepest level shown here, where configuration density grows quickly.
decisions.tradeoff: Keeping the question list visible supports context, but answer configuration must remain clearly subordinate to the selected question.

projects.delivery: Four authoring states connect a blank course to its outline, quiz setup and question configuration. They are presented as team design work within my contribution to course and quiz UI/UX. The primary file is the source; the older copy remains a separate historical reference. Saving, scoring, accessibility and learner behavior require implementation evidence.
projects.outcome: The artifact-backed result is an authoring structure that separates course organization from assessment detail. The screenshots make the hierarchy and its remaining review questions inspectable. No learner-completion, adoption or task-time measurements are available.

journey.question: How do you help a course author build something complex without making every configuration decision compete at once?
journey.opening: The authoring journey starts with a blank course, grows into an outline, then narrows into a quiz and its questions. My contribution sits within Masteriyo’s wider product team. The screens below let the case follow that growing complexity while showing how repeated patterns maintain orientation.
journey.reflection: The useful system is a stable relationship between structure and detail. Section, lesson, quiz and answer are different levels, and the interface has to make the current level obvious. The visible tab highlight and icon-only actions also deserve implementation review: source artifacts are valuable because they expose unfinished decisions as well as strong ones.

evaluation: Ask a course author to create a section, add a lesson and configure a quiz without losing their place in the course outline.
Review question reordering, an invalid answer and cancellation with unsaved changes; verify keyboard access and feedback alongside the visual hierarchy.

projects.title: Mokshya.io
projects.role: Website UX and product communication contribution
projects.summary: A technical product story with an accessible first explanation and a deeper path for people evaluating the mechanism.
context: Mokshya's website needs to serve visitors with different levels of technical knowledge. Someone encountering the product for the first time needs a useful mental model. A developer or evaluator needs enough specificity to investigate further. My contribution centered on information architecture, section sequence and responsive composition.

This case is about protocol-product communication on the website. It should not be read as proof that I designed a complete wallet, implemented the protocol or verified financial outcomes. The existing website preview provides visual context for this contribution.
constraints: The first explanation must be readable without removing the technical distinctions that matter.
Claims need nearby supporting material rather than generic trust language.
Long sections must keep their reading order and relationship to evidence on smaller screens.

decisions.heading: Let the outcome establish relevance
body: I structure the opening around what the product makes possible before asking the visitor to learn its terminology. That gives technical detail a purpose: it answers a question the page has already helped the visitor form.
The trade-off is precision. A short statement should narrow the claim rather than replace an explanation with a sweeping Web3 promise. Where the mechanism matters, the next section must supply it.
decisions.leadIn: Start with the reason a visitor should care.
decisions.tradeoff: Plain language lowers the entry barrier; narrowing the claim preserves technical precision.

decisions.heading: Connect the summary to deeper evaluation
body: An introductory path and a developer path can share one coherent story without requiring the same reading depth. The summary explains the proposition; deeper material exposes the mechanism and the evidence available to inspect.

This is a content-hierarchy decision rather than a measured finding about visitor behavior. I would test whether a newcomer can explain the offer and whether a technical evaluator can find the detail they need without reading the entire page.
decisions.leadIn: Relevance creates the next question: how does this actually work?
decisions.tradeoff: Progressive depth accommodates different readers without forcing everyone through the longest explanation.

decisions.heading: Preserve explanation and proof as a pair
body: A supporting artifact is most useful near the statement it helps assess. On mobile, I keep that relationship in the reading order instead of letting a desktop column arrangement separate the explanation from its supporting visual.
That requires reviewing actual headings, paragraph lengths and image behavior at narrow widths. A responsive page can fit the viewport while still telling its story in an unhelpful order.
decisions.leadIn: The explanation only holds together when its supporting material remains nearby.
decisions.tradeoff: A responsive rearrangement must preserve meaning as well as fit the viewport.

projects.delivery: The portfolio scope is the website's narrative structure, responsive hierarchy and interface composition. The retained website preview provides context; the contribution described here is the narrative structure and interface composition.
projects.outcome: The website account focuses on the order of explanation: establish relevance, then expose the technical mechanism. A first-impression task and a developer-information retrieval task would test those two reading paths. The available material does not include a measured comprehension result.

journey.question: How can a protocol website explain enough for a newcomer without frustrating a technical evaluator?
journey.opening: The website has to introduce an idea before it can ask someone to evaluate a mechanism. My approach connects the opening proposition to deeper technical reading, then keeps explanation and proof together as the layout changes. This case follows that reading path within my website design contribution.
journey.reflection: Each layer should answer the question raised by the previous one. A newcomer and a developer can share the opening without needing the same depth. The strongest editorial structure makes the next useful question easy to pursue.

evaluation: Ask a newcomer to explain the protocol’s purpose after the opening, then find the route to deeper technical information.
Ask a technical evaluator to locate the evidence behind a capability claim without repeatedly returning to the top-level introduction.

projects.title: Designerex
projects.role: Design contribution within a broader marketplace
projects.summary: Balancing image-led fashion discovery with the stable rental information needed to compare listings.
context: Designerex is presented in my existing portfolio as a luxury fashion rental marketplace. The interface has to support interest in a garment and practical evaluation of a rental. Photography can establish desire, but it cannot answer questions about size, availability or terms on its own.

My contribution is limited to browsing and listing patterns, visual hierarchy and the relationship between images and decision details. This case does not claim end-to-end ownership of the marketplace or a measured change in bookings. The account is limited to my part of the browsing and listing experience.
constraints: Large photography needs to coexist with readable listing information.
A comparison grid becomes harder to use when equivalent attributes change position or format.
A team contribution must remain distinct from ownership of the whole product.

decisions.heading: Give the photograph and the metadata different jobs
body: The photograph is the entry point to the item. The repeated listing structure is what lets someone evaluate several items without reconstructing the information every time. I approach the card as a relationship between both, rather than choosing between a purely editorial tile and a specification-heavy product block.
The design trade-off is density. Adding every rental condition to a grid can obscure the garments, while removing every practical attribute pushes too much work into detail pages.
decisions.leadIn: The first job of the listing is to invite a closer look.
decisions.tradeoff: Image prominence creates interest, but essential rental attributes must remain visible.

decisions.heading: Keep comparable information in comparable places
body: Stable labels and placement make the repeated pattern useful. A person should not have to inspect a different part of each card to find an equivalent rental attribute. The detail page can then carry the depth that would overfill the browse view.

A practical review would compare several listings with different image crops, long names and unavailable options. That is a proposed evaluation, not a claim that the current marketplace has passed it.
decisions.leadIn: Interest is not enough to choose a rental; comparable details become the priority.
decisions.tradeoff: Stable card metadata supports comparison; detailed terms belong at a deeper level.

decisions.heading: Keep premium presentation out of the way of the task
body: Visual restraint helps the product remain the focus. Navigation, filtering and actions should support the catalogue instead of demanding their own performance. A quieter interaction convention can still express the brand through typography, spacing and image treatment.

I would inspect keyboard access, filter feedback and returning from a detail page alongside visual craft. A premium browse experience still needs a predictable route back to the person's previous context.
decisions.leadIn: As the person moves into detail and back, interaction must protect the work they have already done.
decisions.tradeoff: Quiet controls support the catalogue while still needing clear focus and active-filter feedback.

projects.delivery: This is a scoped account of marketplace UI contribution. Existing public references are preserved. The public account stays within the contribution and artifacts I can describe without claiming ownership of the whole marketplace.
projects.outcome: The design tension is between image-led browsing and dependable rental comparison. The card and detail hierarchy should be reviewed with varied garment photos, long names and unavailable options. That is the contribution described here, within the broader marketplace team.
related: When polish hides a decision problem

journey.question: How can fashion discovery stay expressive while making rental decisions dependable?
journey.opening: A rental browse journey moves from attraction to comparison. My contribution focuses on that shift: let photography introduce the garment, give recurring details a stable place, and preserve the browsing context as a person explores. The case stays within that contribution to the wider marketplace.
journey.reflection: Premium presentation earns its place when it helps someone judge a garment without hiding the rental decision. Photography creates interest; stable metadata lets a renter turn that interest into a dependable comparison.

evaluation: Ask a renter to compare two garments for occasion, size, price and availability without relying on memory.
Review a long garment name, an unavailable date and a missing photograph to check whether the rental decision remains understandable.

projects.title: Splashnode
projects.category: Technical platform · Website design and frontend
projects.summary: Explaining content, device and data-management capabilities through a website whose design and implementation can inform each other.
context: The existing project material describes Splashnode as a technical platform with content, device and data-management capabilities. The website's job is to help a prospective buyer understand where that platform fits before asking them to compare a long list of features.

My contribution spans website composition, capability explanation, responsive behavior and frontend implementation. This case concerns that website experience. It does not establish ownership of the underlying platform software or provide a verified commercial result.
constraints: Technical capability needs enough explanation to be meaningful to a buyer.
Use cases and feature detail must support each other without repeating the same claim.
Implementation decisions need to preserve hierarchy under real content and viewport constraints.

decisions.heading: Translate a capability into a recognizable task
body: A feature name is only useful when the visitor can connect it to something they need to accomplish. I organize the story around the problem or use case first, then explain the capability that supports it.

That order helps distinguish an introductory promise from the detail needed for evaluation. It also sets an editorial check: if a paragraph could describe any technical platform, it needs a more specific task or a narrower claim.
decisions.leadIn: Begin with the buyer’s task rather than a wall of feature names.
decisions.tradeoff: Use cases make features meaningful; specific mechanism detail prevents the story becoming generic.

decisions.heading: Keep the route to evaluation visible
body: The page should help a visitor decide whether to inspect more detail, view an example or make contact. Repeating the same high-pressure action after every section can interrupt that evaluation instead of supporting it.

I treat action placement as part of the information sequence. A call to action should follow enough context for the visitor to understand what the next step offers, without hiding that route until the end of a long page.
decisions.leadIn: Once the capability is relevant, the visitor needs a way to investigate further.
decisions.tradeoff: Repeated calls to action improve availability but can interrupt evaluation when placed before enough context.

decisions.heading: Let the browser challenge the composition
body: Because my contribution includes frontend work, a layout can be reviewed with actual copy lengths, wrapping and navigation behavior. That feedback is useful while decisions are still easy to change.
The existing public preview is retained as evidence of the work's visual context. The implementation is part of the design discussion, rather than a separate downstream deliverable.
decisions.leadIn: The reading sequence then has to work outside the ideal desktop artboard.
decisions.tradeoff: Reusable sections support implementation while real content may require a deliberate exception.

projects.delivery: The scope joins website UX with implementation-aware composition. Responsive layout, section hierarchy and reusable frontend patterns are part of the same deliverable. Backend platform capability and operational reliability remain outside the evidence shown by this case.
projects.outcome: Design and frontend work meet in the browser: headings wrap, capability sections compete for attention and the route to evaluation has to remain visible. Those are inspectable delivery questions. Usage of the underlying platform and commercial outcomes are outside this website case.

journey.question: How can a technical platform website help a buyer connect capabilities to a real use case?
journey.opening: The design path moves from recognizing a task to understanding a capability and choosing a way to evaluate it. Because my contribution includes frontend work, that path also has to survive real text and browser behavior. The website is the scope of this case, separate from the underlying platform.
journey.reflection: A technical website becomes useful when a visitor can connect the offer to their own job and identify a next step with enough context. Frontend work is valuable here because actual content challenges the composition before it becomes a fixed visual specification.

evaluation: Ask a buyer to connect one platform capability to a task in their own work, then find an appropriate evaluation step.
Review the page with real copy lengths and narrow viewports; check that the use-case explanation still leads naturally into capability detail.

projects.title: Grid Labs
projects.summary: A hosting offer organized around service fit, plan comparison and a clear route to the next commercial step.
context: Grid Labs is a hosting and infrastructure website in the existing portfolio. A prospective buyer needs to understand which service fits, how plans differ and what information is still required before choosing. Specifications matter, but a specification wall does not provide that sequence by itself.

My contribution covers commercial hierarchy, plan presentation, domain-search affordance, responsive layout and static frontend structure. The case is deliberately scoped to the website. A visible search field does not establish a functioning domain lookup, and a plan card does not prove provisioning or billing capability.
constraints: Equivalent plan information needs a consistent order and unit.
Narrow screens make side-by-side comparison difficult.
The interface must remain honest about the difference between a static website and an operating service.

decisions.heading: Make plan differences easy to locate
body: I start with the attributes that change the decision between plans. Those should remain in a stable order so the visitor can compare rather than remember a previous card. Supporting technical detail can remain available without giving every specification equal emphasis.

The review needs realistic prices, units and billing periods. Where current commercial terms are not verified, the portfolio should discuss the comparison pattern instead of repeating potentially outdated offers.
decisions.leadIn: Start by making equivalent plan attributes genuinely comparable.
decisions.tradeoff: A compact plan card supports scanning, while secondary specifications still need a reachable home.

decisions.heading: Treat mobile comparison as an information problem
body: Stacking plan cards preserves content but weakens direct comparison. A useful narrow layout needs stable headings, repeated attribute labels and a clear association between price, period and included capability.

I would test a person comparing two plans with one meaningful difference. If the answer depends on remembering an offscreen card, the layout needs a stronger comparison aid or a more concise set of decision attributes.
decisions.leadIn: That structure faces its hardest test when the plans no longer fit side by side.
decisions.tradeoff: Stacked cards preserve content but weaken direct comparison; repeated labels help maintain context.

decisions.heading: Keep scope visible at the boundary of the site
body: A domain-search affordance can communicate a next step, but it must not imply a service the static implementation does not provide. Its actual destination and response behavior belong in the build review.

The same discipline applies to purchase calls to action. The website should establish what the visitor is continuing toward without inventing a complete account, checkout or hosting-management platform in the case study.
decisions.leadIn: Choosing a plan then leads beyond the limits of the static website.
decisions.tradeoff: A clear commercial affordance must describe its real destination rather than imply an unbuilt service.

projects.delivery: The deliverable is a commercial website and maintainable frontend structure. The public account stays focused on commercial hierarchy, responsive comparison and the limits of a static implementation.
projects.outcome: Plan comparison depends on stable attributes, units and billing periods. The static website scope also limits what a domain-search or purchase affordance can promise. The case centers on those design and implementation boundaries, with current commercial terms left to the service owner.

journey.question: How can a hosting buyer compare plans without carrying every specification in memory?
journey.opening: The journey is a comparison problem before it is a purchase problem. My website contribution organizes the plan differences, considers what happens when cards stack on mobile, and makes the static frontend’s commercial boundary explicit.
journey.reflection: The comparison pattern should reduce the amount of information a buyer has to remember. Stable labels and units are more useful than decorative emphasis on every plan. Provisioning, billing and current offer accuracy remain service-owner responsibilities.

evaluation: Ask a buyer to choose between adjacent plans and explain which specification drove that choice.
Repeat the comparison on a narrow screen with longer plan labels; preserve units and distinctions without requiring horizontal page scrolling.

projects.title: Hamro Idea
projects.category: Software studio · Brand, website and frontend
projects.summary: Connecting a Nepal-based studio's positioning, services, project proof and contact path in one maintainable website.
context: Hamro Idea needed a website that could explain a software studio's offer to a prospective client. The first design question was what a visitor should understand before making contact, not which visual treatment would make the homepage more dramatic.

My existing scope spans positioning, information architecture, responsive UI, reusable sections, semantic markup and frontend implementation. Working across design and code let me inspect the page with real content and adjust its composition before treating the layout as finished.
constraints: Internal service names may not match the language a prospective client uses.
A multi-page site needs repeated patterns without making every service sound identical.
The design must tolerate real copy, image proportions and future content changes.

decisions.heading: Organize the offer around client questions
body: I structure a service page around fit: what problem the service addresses, what work it includes and what proof helps someone evaluate it. That makes the service architecture more useful than a list of internal disciplines.
The practical editorial test is whether a prospect can select a relevant service and explain why it fits. That is a proposed test, not a claim about measured lead quality.

The complete homepage and services page reveal how the offer is introduced and then expanded. These are historical design artifacts with placeholder imagery and copy; their value here is the information sequence, not the sample business claims.
decisions.leadIn: The prospect first needs to recognize a service that fits the problem.
decisions.tradeoff: Client-facing language improves recognition, while precise scope prevents the service promise becoming too broad.

decisions.heading: Keep project proof near the service explanation
body: The About page gives a prospective client another way to evaluate the studio after reading the service offer. Positioning, team presentation and working principles should support the promise made by the earlier pages rather than introduce a disconnected brand story.

I treat that transition as a trust question: what does the visitor still need to understand before starting a conversation? The source contains demonstration imagery and sample claims, so the case discusses their placement and role without presenting them as verified company achievements.
decisions.leadIn: A relevant service creates a reasonable demand for evidence.
decisions.tradeoff: Nearby project proof answers a specific doubt; a large detached gallery makes the visitor connect the dots.

decisions.heading: Make the next conversation easy to start
body: The full contact page brings that evaluation path into a direct request. Name, email and message keep the initial commitment small, while the broader page retains the studio identity and surrounding navigation. The original placeholder content remains visible as part of the historical design.

The artifact also exposes work still needed: prompts must become persistent programmatic labels, the email field needs appropriate input semantics, and validation, submission progress and success feedback need explicit states. Preserving the simple composition requires making those behaviors part of the implementation contract.
decisions.leadIn: After understanding the offer and inspecting relevant work, the prospect needs a clear route to a conversation.
decisions.tradeoff: A short form reduces the information requested upfront, while qualification and useful feedback still need a deliberate interaction design.

projects.delivery: The work joins service information architecture with a static multi-page frontend. The useful handoff is not only a visual style: it includes section responsibilities, responsive rules and a content structure the site can keep using.
projects.outcome: The contribution joins service structure, project proof and a maintainable frontend. I would evaluate it by asking a visitor to choose a service, locate supporting work and reach contact with the right context. Search rankings and inquiry growth are not measured outcomes of this case.
related: Working with a designer in Nepal

journey.question: How can a software studio make its offer understandable and give a prospect a reason to believe it?
journey.opening: The website needs to connect three things that often drift apart: what the studio offers, which work supports that offer, and how a prospect starts a relevant conversation. My design and development contribution brings them into one reading path and a reusable frontend structure.
journey.reflection: Service architecture and implementation meet in the content contract. A new service or longer project description should fit the structure without weakening the story. The case demonstrates the intended relationship between offer, proof and contact; lead quality and search growth need separate measurement.

evaluation: Ask a prospect to choose a relevant service, locate supporting work and reach contact with enough context to describe their need.
Review the form using keyboard input, invalid email, submission failure and success; check persistent labels and meaningful feedback.

projects.title: Zakra Furniture
projects.category: WordPress and Elementor · Furniture starter site
projects.role: Storefront UI and template design contribution
projects.summary: An image-led catalogue designed to remain coherent when real content replaces the demo.
context: A furniture starter site has two users: the shopper browsing products and the site owner changing the catalogue. The initial composition needs to support both. An attractive demo that depends on identical image crops and short product names is a fragile template.

My existing contribution covers catalogue hierarchy, reusable storefront sections, product-card structure, typography, spacing and CMS-aware choices for WordPress and Elementor. This case does not establish ownership of the whole Zakra platform, a working inventory service or a completed ecommerce backend.
constraints: Furniture photography varies in crop, visual weight and aspect ratio.
Product names, category sizes and section counts change after the template is delivered.
Site owners need editing freedom without having to redesign the page for every update.

decisions.heading: Give photography a predictable frame
body: The catalogue needs a repeatable image treatment so a mix of product photographs still reads as one system. The choice is a trade-off: a fixed crop can improve rhythm but remove part of a product, while an uncropped image can create uneven whitespace.
I would review both approaches with varied source images and decide according to the product category. The rule should be explicit rather than dependent on manually preparing every demo asset.
decisions.leadIn: The first source of variation is the photography itself.
decisions.tradeoff: Fixed crops create rhythm but can remove product detail; uncropped images preserve detail with less uniform whitespace.

decisions.heading: Keep the product-card contract stable
body: Names, category cues and decision details need predictable placement. A shopper should not have to relearn a card because a product name wraps onto another line or an optional field is absent.

For a template, that means reviewing long names, missing images, different product counts and narrow layouts. Those cases are part of the design brief for reusable content, not exceptions to be hidden from the portfolio.
decisions.leadIn: A stable image treatment still leaves the rest of the product card to handle change.
decisions.tradeoff: A stable card hierarchy supports scanning without assuming every product has identical content.

decisions.heading: Make editability part of the UX
body: A site owner needs to understand which sections can be repeated, removed or rearranged. Simple spacing and typography rules give the editor useful freedom while limiting accidental visual drift.

The work is therefore more than a single storefront screenshot. Its value lies in the rules that help a catalogue survive ordinary editing. Those rules need to be evaluated with varied catalogue content, rather than judged only against the demo composition.
decisions.leadIn: Those repeated cards belong to sections a site owner needs to edit over time.
decisions.tradeoff: Editing freedom helps the owner; a small set of spacing and type rules limits accidental drift.

projects.delivery: The scope is a reusable starter-site interface and its content behavior. Existing public material is retained. The design discussion stays distinct from claims about checkout, stock accuracy, order fulfillment or sales performance.
projects.outcome: A reusable storefront has to survive ordinary catalogue editing. Varied image crops, longer names and missing optional content are practical tests for the card and section rules described here. A polished demo alone cannot establish checkout or sales performance.

journey.question: How can a furniture starter site remain coherent after a site owner replaces the demo content?
journey.opening: The polished demo is only the starting condition. My template design contribution considers what happens next: mixed photography enters the catalogue, product names wrap, and the site owner changes sections. This case follows those pressures from image treatment to the editing system.
steps: Let the owner change the catalogue
journey.reflection: A template is a set of decisions that someone else keeps using. Its quality becomes clearer under ordinary content variation than under a perfectly art-directed demo. The next review needs varied catalogue fixtures; checkout behavior and sales performance are outside this design account.

evaluation: Replace demo content with long product names, inconsistent photograph proportions and missing descriptions; check that the catalogue hierarchy survives.
Ask a site owner to edit a category and product card, then inspect the result on a narrow screen without manually repairing the layout.

projects.title: Neverwinter Live Parser
projects.summary: Turning an event stream into an inspectable summary without making clean numbers look more certain than the underlying data.
context: A combat parser sits between raw events and a player's explanation of an encounter. The interface needs to group and summarize information while retaining enough context to judge what a number represents. A polished total is not useful if the player cannot tell which encounter, actor, filter or time range produced it.

The public implementation is a Windows-oriented Electron application with a React renderer. Its repository separates parsing, encounter aggregation and renderer view-model tests. My portfolio scope concerns the information model, summary hierarchy and implementation-aware tooling; this is a personal project, separate from ownership of Neverwinter or its game data.
constraints: A summary depends on grouping and calculation assumptions that the interface must not conceal.
Missing or ambiguous events can limit what may safely be inferred.
High-density tables need useful defaults without preventing deeper inspection.

decisions.heading: Keep the summary attached to its context
body: Encounter scope changes the meaning of every number. The renderer view-model tests include a case where a player has 999 total damage across the available data but only 120 in the selected encounter. The expected row uses the selected encounter’s 120 and derives 12 DPS for its ten-second duration. These are fixture values, not player performance claims.

That example makes the interface requirement specific: the selected encounter is part of the metric, and the summary should not silently fall back to a broader total. The linked source is an inspectable contract; this portfolio review has not independently executed that repository’s tests.
decisions.leadIn: A number first needs enough context to be interpreted.
decisions.tradeoff: A compact summary helps orientation but cannot hide the encounter and filter boundaries that define it.

decisions.heading: Separate overview from diagnosis
body: The implementation keeps raw-line parsing, encounter aggregation and renderer row construction in separate source areas. This supports an important distinction: an event’s applied amount, the way events are grouped, and the row a person reads are related but different decisions.

The parser tests specifically distinguish applied damage or healing from base magnitude. The renderer tests then cover ownership grouping, including player-owned summons and companions. An overview must make its grouping understandable so a clean total does not imply a different calculation.
decisions.leadIn: With the context established, the overview should lead into a specific question.
decisions.tradeoff: Progressive detail reduces noise while a clear route to events preserves inspectability.

decisions.heading: Show uncertainty as a state of the data
body: The parser test suite contains an explicit malformed-line case. It expects an issue result and an unknown event type, rather than silently treating the input as valid combat damage. The renderer tests also distinguish zeroed placeholder encounters from encounters with meaningful combat totals.

These source cases give the uncertainty discussion something concrete to point to. They do not prove complete parser accuracy or the way every issue is announced in the UI; that requires execution and inspection of the application with representative logs.
decisions.leadIn: That investigation must also reveal when the source data cannot support an answer.
decisions.tradeoff: Visible uncertainty is less tidy than a zero, but avoids turning missing input into a false conclusion.

code.label: Malformed-input contract from the actual parser test, excerpt

projects.delivery: The public source provides the strongest evidence here: parser cases, encounter aggregation and renderer view-model fixtures can be inspected separately. This review read those contracts and the application manifest; it did not run the Windows application or independently establish calculation accuracy.
projects.outcome: An encounter summary is useful when its actor, time range and supporting events remain inspectable. Known fixtures are the right way to check those relationships and calculation limits. The portfolio account does not substitute a clean dashboard for parser-accuracy evidence.

journey.question: How can a combat summary make complex events readable without hiding the assumptions behind its numbers?
journey.opening: The useful journey is from an encounter overview to the events behind a question. My information-design and frontend work focuses on keeping that connection inspectable, then making incomplete input distinguishable from a real zero. Code and calculation fixtures are the relevant artifacts for this personal tool.
journey.reflection: A clean dashboard is only persuasive when its numbers can be traced back to the relevant events and calculation rules. I would prioritize that traceability over adding another headline statistic. Known input fixtures are required before reporting accuracy or performance improvements.

artifacts: Inspect real parser cases and malformed-input expectations
Inspect encounter-scoped rows and ownership grouping
Read the Electron application and runtime manifest
evaluation: Trace one displayed metric back to known combat events and the documented calculation rule.
Use empty, malformed and interrupted log fixtures before evaluating parsing correctness, session recovery or speed.

projects.title: SassBoilerplate
projects.category: Archived frontend learning · Sass and build workflow
projects.summary: A learning archive that traces a small Sass structure through an existing Gulp-based build, with its upstream origin kept explicit.
context: SassBoilerplate is an earlier frontend learning archive, not an independently authored framework. The archived README identifies it as a historical copy of JR Cologne’s Gulp Starter Kit, with Sass, Pug, Babel, BrowserSync and image-processing tasks. That provenance is part of the project, not a detail to omit from the portfolio.

The useful story is what the files make inspectable: an entry point, a small shared import layer and build tasks that turn authored assets into output. My contribution is presented as learning and adaptation around that workflow, rather than ownership of the upstream kit or a maintained npm package.
constraints: Attribute the original JR Cologne starter kit and preserve its distinction from this learning archive.
Describe the source that exists: the current shared Sass import points to the base rules; empty architecture placeholders were removed.
Historical tooling and dependencies are not a verified recommendation for a new production project.

decisions.heading: Start with the files that actually contribute styles
decisions.leadIn: The entry point gives the first concrete place to inspect the workflow.
body: The archived app.sass imports _includes; _includes imports base/_base. That is a small, visible dependency path. The source comments explicitly say that empty helper, module, partial and global placeholders were removed, so the case should not describe a large token or component architecture that is no longer there.
The design principle is legibility: a file’s name and import should explain its responsibility. For this archive, the honest example is a short chain a reader can inspect directly.
decisions.tradeoff: A small import layer is easy to follow; adding categories before they own real styles creates structure without a useful responsibility.

code.label: Actual entry and shared import, excerpted from the learning archive

decisions.heading: Read the build as a sequence of responsibilities
decisions.leadIn: After locating the Sass source, the next question is how it becomes browser output.
body: The archived sassTask reads Sass and SCSS, initializes source maps, handles errors, resolves dependents, compiles, prefixes and minifies CSS, writes maps and sends the result to the output directory and BrowserSync. Separate named tasks handle templates, JavaScript, images and copied dependencies.

Those boundaries make the workflow easier to explain than a list of tools alone. They also expose where a modern migration needs care: an old compiler or image dependency can fail even when the Sass source itself is simple.
decisions.tradeoff: Automation removes repetitive work, while every additional transform introduces another compatibility and debugging boundary.

decisions.heading: Treat the archive as evidence of learning
decisions.leadIn: The last decision is how to present and reuse the work responsibly.
body: The archived README names the upstream package, original author, repository and MIT license. It also warns that the historical Node requirement and dependencies do not establish compatibility with a current runtime. That is the appropriate boundary for this portfolio entry.

The artifact is useful for explaining how I learned to connect source organization and build behavior. It is not a new framework release, a currently maintained package, or evidence of measured developer onboarding gains.
decisions.tradeoff: Keeping historical work shows the learning path, provided its attribution and present-day limits remain clear.

projects.delivery: A public learning archive with inspectable Sass imports and named Gulp build tasks. The original starter kit is credited to JR Cologne. This review inspected the source and documentation; it did not install or execute the historical dependency tree.
projects.outcome: The archive supports a concrete explanation of source ownership, import direction and build responsibilities. Its value in the portfolio is the learning and adaptation, with upstream attribution and maintenance limits visible.

journey.question: What did a small starter workflow teach me about making frontend structure understandable?
journey.opening: This case is a deliberately modest learning story. Start at the Sass entry, follow the shared import into base rules, then look at how the build transforms the files. The archive makes that path inspectable without turning a borrowed starter into a claim of original framework authorship.
steps: Keep the archive in its proper scope
journey.reflection: The useful lesson is to make responsibility and provenance easy to follow. A starter can support learning without needing to become a product claim. Today I would review a small maintained toolchain against the actual project rather than recommend this historical dependency set unchanged.

artifacts: Read the archive status and upstream attribution
Inspect the actual named build tasks
evaluation: Ask a developer unfamiliar with the archive to locate the source styles, build entry point and generated output.
Review upstream attribution and dependency age before deciding what can be learned from the structure or reused in a maintained project.
